Table row 1 from Perspectives on the relationship between materials chemistry and roll-to-roll electrode manufacturing for high-energy lithium-ion batteries, page 1:
The current ultimate U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Vehicle Technologies Office (VTO) cell cost target is $80/kWh.

Table row 24 from Perspectives on the relationship between materials chemistry and roll-to-roll electrode manufacturing for high-energy lithium-ion batteries, page 4:
Electrode and cell manufacturing costs are approximately 1/3 the combined cost of the anode, cathode, separator, electrolyte, and Cu foil material costs according to a basic analysis using the Argonne National Laboratory BatPaC model. This ultimate cell cost target must be met while simultaneously achieving 500 Wh/kg energy density, 800 W/kg power density, and 10-15 min fast charging times, which is a daunting task.

Table row 14 from Perspectives on the relationship between materials chemistry and roll-to-roll electrode manufacturing for high-energy lithium-ion batteries, page 3:
The higher the line speed of the coating process, the more difficult obtaining uniform electrode architectures becomes, as coating defects become more prominent such as streaking, pinholes, agglomeration, etc. [5,6] Once high-quality electrodes are produced, they must also be assembled into pouch or cylindrical cells with care and formed under time consuming cycling conditions [2,7].

Table row 27 from Perspectives on the relationship between materials chemistry and roll-to-roll electrode manufacturing for high-energy lithium-ion batteries, page 4:
The current manufacturing costs are about double this figure [14].

The difference between the US Department of Energy cell cost target of $80/kWh and the cited 2020 battery cost of $160/kWh is $80/kWh.
